```{r}
size_data$climate <- as.factor(size_data$climate)
size_data$species <- as.factor(size_data$species)
size_data$tree_id <- as.factor(size_data$tree_id)
size_data$time <- as.numeric(size_data$time) 
```


```{r}
summary(size_data)
```
## Model with Slope Explanation:

We are modeling pear size over time, accounting for:

Fixed effects: time, climate, species

Random effects: variability among individual pears (pear_id), optionally allowing each pear to grow at its own rate (random slope)

Explanation: Allows each pear to have its own starting size (intercept) and growth rate (slope over time).

More flexible, captures individual growth trajectories.

Warning: boundary (singular) fit: This means the model might be too complex — the variance of the slope might be close to zero or highly correlated with the intercept (as we see here: correlation = -1.00). 
* A singular fit occurs when one or more random effects are estimated to have:
* Variance ≈ 0 (i.e., not contributing anything to the model), or
* Perfect or near-perfect correlation with another random effect (e.g., correlation = ±1.00).

* Variance for slope is small (0.01246), possibly unidentifiable.
* Lower REML(Restricted Maximum Likelihood) = 14217.8 means
## Model Interpretion: 
Time: Highly significant positive effect → pears grow ~0.51 cm/week.

Climate Scenarios: Scenario 2 and 3 significantly reduce growth compared to Scenario 1.

Species: Doyenne pears are ~0.89 cm smaller than baseline (Conference).

```{r}
# 4. Fit Linear Mixed Models

## 4a. Random intercept model (basic model)
model1 <- lmer(size ~ 0 + time : climate : species + (0 + time | pear_id), data = size_data)
summary(model1)

```
```{r}
growth_model_lmer <- lmer(
  size ~ 0 + species : climate : time + (0 + time  | pear_id),
  data    = size_data
)
print(drop1(growth_model_lmer))
summary(growth_model_lmer)
```

```{r}
summary_output <- summary(growth_model_lmer)
fixed_effects <- summary_output$coefficients

fixed_effects_df <- as.data.frame(fixed_effects)
fixed_effects_df$bonf_p <- p.adjust(fixed_effects_df$`Pr(>|t|)`, method = "bonferroni")
print(fixed_effects_df)

```

```{r}
library(emmeans)

emm <- emmeans(growth_model_lmer, ~ species * climate)

comparison_results <- contrast(emm, method = "pairwise", adjust = "bonferroni")

summary(comparison_results)


```
```{r}
library(multcomp)
mcp_test <- glht(growth_model_lmer, linfct = mcp(species = "Tukey"))
summary(mcp_test, test = adjusted("bonferroni"))

```


```{r}

```
## Simple Model Explanation 
*Allows each pear to have a different starting size only.
*Assumes same growth rate over time for all pears.
## Output 
*Higher REML = 16099.4 → worse fit than Model 1.
*No singular fit warning → more stable, but less flexible.

## Model interpretation 
Similar interpretation, but:
*Species Doyenne now has a stronger negative effect (1.89 cm smaller).
*Slightly stronger climate scenario effects (Scenario 2 and 3 more negative).


## Conclusion 
Model 1 fits better, but the singular fit suggests that the random slope for time may not be needed or that the model is too complex for your data.

```{r}
model2 <- lmer(size ~ time + climate + species + (1| pear_id), data = size_data)
summary(model2)
```

## Uncorrelated Model Explanation
*This model allows time to vary by pear, but doesn’t estimate the correlation with the intercept.
*It’s a simpler and more stable version of Model 1

##Benefits
*No singular fit
*Lower REML/AIC
*Reasonable variance estimates

##Model fit:

* The REML criterion (14422.1) is higher than the correlated slope model (14217.8) but much lower than the simple model (16099.4), indicating it's a good compromise.
* No singular fit warning, so the model is statistically sound.

##Fixed effects:

*Time is still a strong, significant positive predictor of size.
*The effect of climate scenarios is no longer significant (p > 0.05), suggesting the differences between them might not be strong once random variation in growth is modeled properly.
*Species effect remains significant (Doyenne leads to smaller size).

##Random effects:

There's clear variability between trees in both starting size (intercept) and growth rate over time (slope for time), but they're not correlated, which avoids the previous overfitting problem.

```{r}
model_uncorrelated <- lmer(size ~ time + climate + species + (1 | pear_id) + (0 + time | pear_id), data = size_data)
summary(model_uncorrelated)
```

```{r}
model_doublepipe <- lmer(size ~ time + climate + species + (time || pear_id), data = size_data)

summary(model_doublepipe)
```

```{r}
anova(model2, model_uncorrelated)
```

```{r}
anova(model2, model_doublepipe)
```

```{r}
library(ggeffects)
library(ggplot2)

# Get predicted values for time and climate
preds <- ggpredict(model_uncorrelated, terms = c("time", "climate"))

# Plot
ggplot(preds, aes(x = x, y = predicted, color = group)) +
  geom_line(size = 1.2) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high, fill = group), alpha = 0.2, color = NA) +
  labs(title = "Predicted Pear Size Over Time by Climate Scenario",
       x = "Time (Weeks)", y = "Predicted Size (cm)",
       color = "Climate", fill = "Climate") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
# Get predicted values for time and species
pred_species <- ggpredict(model_uncorrelated, terms = c("time", "species"))

# Plot
ggplot(pred_species, aes(x = x, y = predicted, color = group)) +
  geom_line(size = 1.2) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high, fill = group), alpha = 0.2, color = NA) +
  labs(title = "Predicted Pear Size Over Time by Species",
       x = "Time (Weeks)", y = "Predicted Size (cm)",
       color = "Species", fill = "Species") +
  theme_minimal()
```


* Lower AIC/BIC values indicate a better model fit with a penalty for complexity.
If Model 1 (with random slopes) has substantially lower AIC/BIC, it's worth keeping.


14217.8

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# Calculate mean size per week per climate
mean_size_by_group <- size_data %>%
  group_by(time, climate) %>%
  summarise(mean_size = mean(size), .groups = "drop")

# Plot manually
ggplot(mean_size_by_group, aes(x = time, y = mean_size, color = climate)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Average Pear Size Over Time by Climate Scenario",
       x = "Week",
       y = "Mean Size (cm)",
       color = "Climate Scenario") +
  theme_minimal()

```

```{r}

# Calculate mean size by time, climate, and species
mean_size_species <- size_data %>%
  group_by(time, climate, species) %>%
  summarise(mean_size = mean(size), .groups = "drop")

# Plot with facets
ggplot(mean_size_species, aes(x = time, y = mean_size, color = climate)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ species) +
  labs(title = "Pear Size Over Time by Climate Scenario and Species",
       x = "Week", y = "Mean Size (cm)") +
  theme_minimal()


```

```{r}

# 1) Compute the mean size per week × scenario × species
mean_growth <- size_data %>%
  group_by(time, climate, species) %>%
  summarise(mean_size = mean(size, na.rm = TRUE), .groups="drop")
View(mean_growth)

# 2) Plot with scenario→color and species→linetype
ggplot(mean_growth, aes(
  x        = time,
  y        = mean_size,
  color    = climate,
  linetype = species,
  group    = interaction(climate, species)
)) +
  geom_line(size = 1) +
  scale_color_brewer(
    palette = "Set2",
    name    = "Scenario"
  ) +
  scale_linetype_manual(
    values = c("Conference" = "solid",
               "Doyenne"    = "dashed"),
    name   = "Species"
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Mean Pear Growth Curves by Scenario and Species",
    x        = "Week",
    y        = "Mean Diameter (cm)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "right",
    axis.text.x    = element_text(size = 8)
  )

```

```{r}
library(reshape2)
heat_data <- size_data %>%
  group_by(time, climate) %>%
  summarise(mean_size = mean(size), .groups = "drop") %>%
  dcast(time ~ climate, value.var = "mean_size")

# Melt again for ggplot heatmap
heat_data_melt <- melt(heat_data, id.vars = "time")

ggplot(heat_data_melt, aes(x = time, y = variable, fill = value)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  labs(title = "Heatmap of Mean Pear Size",
       x = "Week", y = "Climate Scenario", fill = "Mean Size") +
  theme_minimal()

```
